guideTitle: Best Craftsman and Comparable Wood Chippers (2026)
metaTitle: Best Craftsman and Similar Wood Chippers
metaDescription: Craftsman gas and electric chippers compared with Yardmax, Earthquake, MechMaxx Honda and EFCUT models on engine, branch capacity and warranty terms.
expertTake: The gas Craftsman with a 196cc Kohler engine is the best all round pick for a 3 inch chipper, because it pairs a 20:1 reduction ratio with a split warranty and a brand with parts support. The electric Craftsman is a good small-yard tool, but only for limbs under 1.5 inches. The MechMaxx with a Honda engine is the one to buy for 4 inch limbs. If you only prune shrubs, skip gas machines altogether.
introParagraphs: A chipper is judged by the engine that drives it, the blades that cut and the way it handles a jam. Small-engine chippers look similar from the outside, but engine brand, blade design and drive layout decide how they behave after a year of ownership and how often they bog on a thick limb.

This guide compares engine-led chippers from several makers, including models that use well-known engine brands. It explains the specs that matter and how to size a machine to your trees. Start with the picks above for the short list, then read the reviews below to find the match for your yard.

products.name: Craftsman 3 In 6.5HP Kohler Gas Wood Chipper Shredder
products.description:
The gas Craftsman is the better of the two Craftsman chippers for anyone with real limbs to deal with. A 196cc Kohler engine rated at 6.5HP turns two heat-treated chipper blades and four integrated shredder hammers, and the listing quotes a 20:1 reduction ratio, higher than the 15:1 on most generic 7HP machines. The single-stream design sends chips and shredded material out of one path instead of two.

Practical design choices help. A removable hopper makes it easier to reach the rotor for cleaning and blade work, and an elevated side discharge chute keeps chips from burying the wheels. A 3 inch branch capacity is the standard for this class. Against the electric Craftsman, which takes only 1.5 inches, this machine handles twice the diameter, and against the Yardmax it adds a stated reduction ratio and a split warranty of 2 years on the engine and 1 year on workmanship.

Ownership is that of a small gas engine. Use fresh fuel with stabilizer, change the oil after the first few hours and check the blade sharpness each season. Kohler engines have wide parts and dealer coverage, which makes a small engine easier to keep running in year five than an unbranded one. Dry branches chip cleanly, while green, leafy material will wrap the shredder hammers and slow the machine.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a name-brand 3 inch chipper with a Kohler engine and an elevated discharge.
pros: Kohler 196cc engine has wide parts and dealer support
20:1 reduction ratio beats the typical 15:1 of generic units
Removable hopper makes blade and rotor access easier
Two year engine warranty with a one year workmanship cover
cons: 3 inch limit is the same as on the cheaper 7HP machines
Engine is smaller than the 301cc unit on the Earthquake K33
Shredder hammers can clog on wet green leaves and stems

products.name: Craftsman CMXGPXT1500 15 Amp Steel Electric Wood Chipper
products.description:
The electric Craftsman is a light-duty machine for twigs and prunings, and it is honest about it with a 1.5 inch rating. A 15 amp, 120V motor spins heat-treated steel blades at up to 4,500 RPM, a higher blade speed than the 3,700 to 4,000 RPM seen on many rivals. Built-in overload protection shuts the motor down if it is overworked, which protects it from a stalled blade.

Never-flat 7 inch wheels and a push-down handle make it easy to move and tuck away. A hopper-lock knob opens the hopper for cleaning, and a collection bag comes in the box. Compared with the gas Craftsman, you give up half the branch diameter and gain quiet, no fuel and no engine upkeep. Against the Yardmax and Earthquake, which are gas machines for 3 inch limbs, this is a different tool for a different yard.

The power supply decides performance. Use a 12 gauge extension cord and keep it short, because a thin cord starves the motor under load. Avoid wet green material and leaves, which wrap the blade, and clean the hopper after each session. It suits a small garden and a homeowner who wants a quiet cleanup tool, not someone who is clearing storm damage.
products.bestFor: Small yards with light pruning where a quiet plug-in machine is enough.
pros: Blade speed up to 4,500 RPM is high for a 15 amp unit
Never-flat wheels mean no tire to repair or inflate
Overload protection guards the motor against a stalled blade
No fuel, oil or carburetor to maintain through the winter
cons: 1.5 inch limit is the smallest capacity in this lineup
Tied to a heavy gauge cord and a nearby power outlet
Not suited to green limbs or big storm cleanup work

products.name: Yardmax YW6065 2-in-1 Chipper Shredder with Kohler Engine

specList.label: Construction
specList.value: All steel, including hopper and intake

specList.label: Shredder
specList.value: Two J hammers and two rectangular hammers

products.description:
The Yardmax YW6065 is the old-school choice in this lineup, built around all steel construction including the hopper and intake. Where the cheaper plastic-bodied machines can crack or warp, steel takes knocks, and the direct drive engine power gives constant self-feeding chipping with no lag. A Kohler 2000 series engine gives it the power for branches up to 3 inches.

Cutting hardware is two 2 inch chipping knives and a shredding set of two J hammers and two rectangular hammers, a hardware mix that cuts wood to size and mulches it. Against the Craftsman gas model, the Yardmax has no stated reduction ratio and a less detailed listing, but it shares the Kohler engine brand and the 3 inch capacity. The listing is brief, so verify the bag and warranty details on the product page.

Steel adds weight, which makes it a machine you leave in one place or tow, but also means it lasts. Keep the knives sharp, check hammer wear and clean the hopper to prevent rust. A direct drive machine runs the rotor whenever the engine runs, so always shut it down before clearing a jam. Use fresh fuel and change the oil after the first few hours.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a steel machine with a Kohler engine and plan to keep it for many seasons.
pros: All steel construction including hopper and intake
Kohler 2000 series engine with wide parts and dealer support
Direct drive gives constant self-feeding chipping with no lag
Two J hammers and two rectangular hammers shred twigs
cons: Listing is brief and omits reduction ratio and warranty
Steel body is heavier to move than the plastic bodied rivals
Direct drive means the blades spin whenever it runs

products.name: Earthquake K33 301cc 3 In Chipper Shredder

specList.label: Shredder
specList.value: Tri-Hammers and J-hammers in the rotor

products.description:
The Earthquake K33 has the biggest engine of the 3 inch machines at 301cc, well above the 196cc Kohler on the Craftsman. A larger engine means more torque reserve when a dense limb hits the blade, so it is less likely to bog on seasoned hardwood. It handles branches up to 3 inches in the chipper cone and shreds twigs and leaves in a top hopper using a series of Tri-Hammers and J-hammers.

Handling is better than most. Large 11 inch never-flat wheels roll over lawn and gravel, and a Dock-and-Lock bag attaches without a struggle. The footprint is a compact 29.9 inches square, so it fits in a shed. Compared with the Craftsman gas model, you gain engine size and bag design, but lose the stated reduction ratio and split warranty detail, and the price tier is higher.

Ownership is the same small engine routine, with bigger oil and fuel needs. Use fresh fuel, check the oil before every session and sharpen the blades each season. A bigger engine makes more noise, so wear hearing protection. For anyone who cuts mostly small prunings, the extra engine is wasted, but for limbs at the 3 inch limit it is the machine least likely to stall.
products.bestFor: Buyers who cut seasoned 3 inch limbs often and want engine torque in reserve.
pros: 301cc engine gives the most torque reserve of the 3 inch units
Large 11 inch never-flat wheels roll easily over rough ground
Dock-and-Lock bag attaches and releases quickly and cleanly
Compact footprint of about 30 inches square fits a shed
cons: Costs more than the 7HP machines of the same capacity
Larger engine adds weight, noise and fuel use to every job
Listing gives no reduction ratio or warranty detail

products.name: MechMaxx GS650 4 In Honda 196cc Towable Wood Chipper

specList.label: Blades
specList.value: 2 blades and 1 anvil, CR alloy steel

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Emergency stop button by the feed port

products.description:
The MechMaxx GS650 puts a Honda 196cc engine behind a 4 inch chipper, and that engine choice is the reason to consider it. Honda small engines have a long record for starting reliably after storage and for parts availability, which matters on a machine you may not run for six months. It takes branches up to 4 inches through a drum with two blades and an anvil, with a 20:1 reduction ratio.

The rest of the machine is built for moving around a property. A tow bar and two 14 inch wheels allow towing behind a lawn tractor, a 360 degree rotary discharge chute and adjustable deflector aim chips, and an emergency stop button sits next to the feed port. Compared with the Craftsman gas model, it takes an extra inch of limb and uses a Honda instead of a Kohler engine, but it is a much more expensive machine.

The 6.5HP Honda is smaller than the 9HP EFCUT, so near the 4 inch limit you must use dry limbs and feed slowly. Keep the blade and anvil gap correct, check the oil often and use fresh fuel. The warranty is 2 years on the machine and 2 years on the engine. For most homeowners the Craftsman 3 inch model is enough, but for a larger property the Honda unit is the quality choice.
products.bestFor: Property owners who want 4 inch capacity and a Honda engine with a long starting record.
pros: Honda 196cc engine is known for reliable starting and parts
Takes 4 inch branches, one inch more than the Craftsman
Emergency stop sits right beside the feed port for fast use
Two year warranty covers both the machine and the engine
cons: Priced like a premium machine compared with the Craftsman
6.5HP engine is modest for dense limbs near 4 inches
Larger and heavier than the 3 inch units in this lineup

products.name: EFCUT C40E 4 In Electric Start 9HP Wood Chipper

specList.label: Flywheel
specList.value: 15.9 in with long high-speed steel blades

products.description:
The EFCUT C40E is the 4 inch machine for people who dislike pull cords. A key electric start fires a 9HP, 274cc engine, which is the largest of the 4 inch machines here and a much bigger power reserve than the 196cc Honda or Kohler engines. A 15.9 inch flywheel and long high-speed steel blades give it the momentum to chip 4 inch limbs.

The reduction ratio is 15:1, lower than the 20:1 on the Craftsman gas model and the MechMaxx, so you get more bulk in the bag. A spacious hopper and an adjustable discharge chute help with loading and aiming, and the machine is EPA and CARB certified. The warranty is 1 year after registration and excludes blades and consumables, shorter than the 2 years from MechMaxx.

Electric start means a battery to keep charged, so connect a maintainer in winter and expect to replace it every few years. Use fresh fuel, check the oil before every run and sharpen the blades each season. For a person who runs a chipper a few times per year, a pull-start machine is simpler, but for frequent stop and start jobs the key start is a real convenience.
products.bestFor: Owners with heavy limbs who want a big engine and key starting instead of a pull cord.
pros: Key electric start removes the cold-weather pull cord
9HP 274cc engine is the largest in this comparison
15.9 inch flywheel stores momentum for 4 inch limbs
EPA and CARB certified for states with emission rules
cons: One year warranty excludes blades and other consumable parts
The start battery needs charging and eventual replacement
Lower 15:1 reduction ratio than the 20:1 on the rivals

buyingCriteria.explanation: Electric chippers such as the Craftsman CMXGPXT1500 take limbs up to about 1.5 inches and run quietly from an outlet, while gas machines take 3 to 4 inches. The deciding fact is the thickest limb you prune, not the number of limbs. A machine at the top of its range jams often, so size up by about half an inch from your thickest regular limb. Many buyers pick electric for convenience and then find that a single thick limb makes it useless.

Engine brand affects starting, parts and service. The gas Craftsman and the Yardmax use Kohler engines, the MechMaxx GS650 uses a Honda 196cc, and the Earthquake uses a 301cc Viper engine. A branded engine makes parts easier to find five years later. Unbranded engines may work well, but you rely on the seller for support. If the machine will sit through winter, a branded engine with an easy-start carburetor reduces spring frustration.

Capacity is the thickest limb the chute is rated for, and it applies to dry softwood. The Craftsman gas, Yardmax and Earthquake list 3 inches, while the MechMaxx and EFCUT list 4 inches. Green hardwood is much harder, and a 6.5HP engine will bog on it near the limit. Treat the rating as a ceiling and plan to chip dry limbs fed butt end first.

The Craftsman gas and the MechMaxx list 20:1, while the EFCUT lists 15:1. A higher ratio means fewer bags to empty, but ratios are measured on ideal debris. The hardware matters too: the Craftsman uses four hammers and the Yardmax two J and two rectangular hammers. Hammers shred twigs and leaves, so more hammers produce finer output.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Judge warranty and what it excludes
buyingCriteria.explanation: The Craftsman gas offers 2 years on the engine and 1 year on workmanship, the MechMaxx offers 2 years on machine and engine and the EFCUT offers 1 year excluding blades. Blades and consumables are usually excluded, so budget for replacements. A warranty is only as good as the seller, so register the machine promptly.

Pull start is simple and has no battery, while key electric start like the EFCUT C40E adds convenience and a battery to maintain. A gas machine needs fuel stabilizer or an empty carburetor over winter. Electric machines like the electric Craftsman skip that and store in a corner. Check the folded or stored size, since the Earthquake K33 is about 30 inches square.

specDecoder.meaning: Displacement in cc describes the engine's cylinder volume and horsepower is the maker's output rating. The 196cc Kohler and Honda engines are rated at about 6.5HP, the 274cc EFCUT at 9HP and the 301cc Earthquake larger still. Larger engines carry more torque reserve for dense limbs.
specDecoder.watchFor: HP ratings are gross engine figures. Engine brand and quality matter as much as the number.

specDecoder.meaning: The maximum limb diameter the chute can accept, rated on dry softwood. It depends on chute size, blade length and engine torque.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 1.5 inch capacity of the electric Craftsman and the 4 inch capacity of the MechMaxx are ceilings, not daily working sizes.

specDecoder.meaning: The reduction ratio compares the original debris volume to the chip volume. A 20:1 ratio means twenty piles shrink to one, which depends on blade sharpness and material.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 20:1 on the Craftsman gas and MechMaxx is a best case. Wet or leafy debris reduces it.

specDecoder.meaning: In a direct drive machine the engine shaft turns the rotor with no belt or clutch. The Yardmax is described as direct drive, which gives constant self feeding with no lag. It has fewer wear parts but the blades spin whenever the engine runs.
specDecoder.watchFor: Always stop the engine and wait for the rotor to stop before reaching into the chute.

specDecoder.meaning: These are US and California emission standards for small engines. A certified engine can be sold in all states. The EFCUT C40E is listed as certified.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some listings say not for California sale. Check the page if you live in a state with strict rules.

howWeEvaluated.title: Engine and brand support
howWeEvaluated.description: We ranked machines by engine size and brand, from the 196cc Kohler on the Craftsman gas to the 301cc Earthquake. We counted Honda and Kohler engines as a plus for parts and starting. We noted listings that gave engine details and those that did not.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated branch capacity, blade count and hammer count. The Craftsman gas, Yardmax and Earthquake share 3 inches, and the MechMaxx and EFCUT reach 4 inches. We favored machines with a stated reduction ratio and an accessible rotor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Warranty and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed warranty terms in order, from the 2 years on the Craftsman engine and MechMaxx to the 1 year on the EFCUT. We read exclusions and noted that blades are usually excluded. Machines with sparse listings lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wheels, footprint, towing and bag design. The Earthquake's 11 inch never-flat wheels and Dock-and-Lock bag and the MechMaxx tow bar lead. The electric Craftsman's never-flat wheels and push-down handle suit tight storage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety and fit to a yard
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at emergency stops, overload protection and hopper locks. The MechMaxx has an emergency stop, the electric Craftsman has overload protection and a hopper lock, and the gas Craftsman has a removable hopper. We matched each machine to the size of yard and limb it suits.

howToChoose.intro: The difference is convenience against maintenance.

cards.label: Pull start
cards.text: The Craftsman gas, Yardmax, Earthquake and MechMaxx Honda use a recoil start. There is no battery to maintain, and with fresh fuel and a clean carburetor they start in a few pulls. They suit occasional users.

cards.label: Electric start
cards.text: The EFCUT C40E has a key electric start that fires the 9HP engine without a pull. It helps in cold weather and for stop and start work, but the battery needs charging and replacement. It suits frequent users with big limbs.

howToChoose.note: Pick pull start for seasonal use and simplicity. Pick electric start if you chip often or have trouble pulling a cord.

howToChoose.intro: What backs the engine matters in year three.

rows: Craftsman 3 In Gas or Yardmax YW6065

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A large property produces regular limbs of 2 to 4 inches and benefits from a towable machine, a reliable engine and a large discharge. An emergency stop and a rear or side clean-out matter for repeated use.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The MechMaxx GS650 Honda is the best fit because of its 4 inch capacity, tow bar and emergency stop. The Earthquake K33 is the better choice if you prefer a 3 inch machine with a large engine and big wheels.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you chip often or cut limbs near the limit. The MechMaxx Honda and the Earthquake K33 give engine reserve, and the Craftsman gas adds a warranty and a branded engine.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you only prune once a season. The electric Craftsman and the Yardmax cover light work without the cost of a bigger engine.

maintenance.interval: After the first 5 hours, then every season
maintenance.why: New engines shed metal early. Fresh oil protects bearings in an air-cooled engine.
Dull blades tear wood and strain the engine. Keep the blade and anvil gap correct.
Vibration loosens bolts and wears hammers. A loose part can damage the rotor.
Chipping dust clogs the filter. A dirty filter makes the engine run rich.
Stale ethanol fuel gums the carburetor. A dry carburetor starts first time.
A flat battery cannot turn the engine. A maintainer extends life.

faq.q: Should I buy the electric or the gas Craftsman?
faq.a: Buy the electric Craftsman if your limbs are under 1.5 inches and you have an outlet nearby. Buy the gas Craftsman if you cut limbs up to 3 inches or work away from power. The gas machine needs fuel and oil care, and the electric one needs a heavy gauge extension cord.

faq.q: Is a Kohler or Honda engine better?
faq.a: Both are respected, and the practical difference is parts and dealer coverage. Honda has a long record for starting after storage, and Kohler is common on outdoor power equipment. Either is a better long-term bet than an unbranded engine.

faq.q: Why is the reduction ratio different between models?
faq.a: The ratio depends on blade and hammer design and on how finely the machine chops. The Craftsman gas and MechMaxx list 20:1, while the EFCUT lists 15:1. It is measured on ideal material, so treat it as a comparison figure.
You can, but green wood is heavy with moisture and tends to jam. It chips more cleanly after a few weeks of drying. Feed it butt end first and keep the machine well below its limit.
If you chip often or have trouble with a pull cord, yes. It adds a battery to maintain. For a few uses a year, a pull-start machine is simpler.

faq.q: How should I store a gas chipper over winter?
faq.a: Add fuel stabilizer and run the engine for a few minutes, or drain the tank and run the carburetor dry. Change the oil, clean the chute, oil the blades lightly and cover the machine. This prevents gummed fuel and rust.
